abstract: Climate change is expected to increase the frequency, duration and intensity of weather events that cause desiccation stress to small-bodied terrestrial insects. Whether a desiccation event may cause mortality depends on the time-dependent osmo- and ionoregulation responses of insects to desiccation and their recovery. Yet these responses and their associated energetic costs are not always clear for a range of mesic species. Here, we characterised the ability of house crickets (Acheta domesticus) to physiologically resist and recover from desiccation. We measured water loss from different tissues, changes in haemolymph volume and in haemolymph ion concentration as well as stored macromolecules (lipids, carbohydrates and proteins) use over a time-course of desiccation (0, 3, 6 or 18 h) and recovery with access to water and with or without access to food (18 h desiccation and 6 h recovery). During 18 h of desiccation, crickets regulated haemolymph ion concentration, avoiding hyperkalaemia and hypernatraemia, despite losing up to 14.5 and 21.1% of their body water for female and males respectively, across all body compartments. Recovery represented a distinct physiological phase to acute stress with a restoration of ion concentrations and body water with significant energetic contributions from stored macromolecules. We conclude crickets employ a general two-phase physiological strategy to withstand and recover from a short-term acute desiccation stress, establishing a physiological baseline to evaluate potential desiccation stress, and providing key insight into the time-dependency of osmoregulation and ion regulation for insects encountering fluctuating desiccation stress under climate change.
